stimuli.title: Glasses for working hands
stimuli.content:
Somewhere in their forties, most people notice a small but annoying change. The print in the newspaper seems smaller than it used to be, and they begin to hold their phones further away to read a message. This is presbyopia, the gradual loss of the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects. It is not a disease. It happens to almost everyone with age, because the lens inside the eye slowly becomes less flexible.

For an office worker in a city, the remedy is simple: a visit to an optician and a pair of reading glasses. For many people in villages and small towns, however, the change can quietly damage their livelihood. A tailor who cannot see the eye of a needle, a weaver who can no longer follow a fine pattern, or a farmer who cannot sort seeds may work more slowly and earn less, often in the very years when their skills are at their best.

What makes this loss especially sad is how easily it can be prevented. Simple reading glasses are among the cheapest of all medical aids. In most cases a trained health worker with a basic reading chart can find the right strength in a few minutes.

The difficulty lies in reaching people. Many have never had their eyes tested, and some believe that weak near vision is simply a part of growing old that must be accepted. Others worry that glasses will make their eyes lazy, or feel embarrassed to wear them in front of their neighbours.

Several voluntary groups now hold eye camps at weekly markets and village fairs, where people can try on glasses and take home a pair that suits them. Organisers say the reaction is often the same. A woman threads a needle at the first attempt, or an old shopkeeper reads his account book without squinting, and then laughs in surprise. For a small cost, years of good work are given back.

stimuli.title: Paths that walkers choose
stimuli.content:
Walk through almost any park or college campus and you will find them: narrow strips of bare earth cutting across the grass, often running at an angle between two paved paths. Nobody planned them. They were made by thousands of people who decided, one step at a time, that the official route was too long. Planners call them 'desire lines' or 'desire paths'.

Such paths appear for a simple reason. Most people, when they are in a hurry, take the shortest route they can see. If a paved path turns a corner at a right angle, walkers will cut the corner. Once a few have done so, the grass wears thin, a faint line becomes visible, and others follow it, so that within weeks the faint track becomes a clear one.

For a long time, the usual response was to fight the walkers. Park managers put up fences, planted hedges or added signs asking people to keep off the grass. These measures rarely worked for long. A fence would be stepped over or a gap would be pushed through a hedge, and the path would reappear a little further along.

Some planners now take the opposite view. Instead of treating desire paths as damage, they treat them as information. A path worn across a lawn shows exactly where people want to go, which is something no drawing can predict with certainty. Some have even suggested waiting until a new campus has been in use for a few months before laying its walkways, so that the paved paths can follow the tracks that appear.

The idea reaches beyond parks. Designers of websites, offices and public services face the same question: should people be made to follow the route that was planned for them, or should the route be redrawn to follow people? Desire paths suggest that when many people keep ignoring a design, the fault may lie with the design rather than with the people.

stimuli.title: The pot that is auctioned
stimuli.content:
In many Indian towns, long before banks reached every street, families saved and borrowed through the chit fund. The idea is simple. Suppose twenty people agree to pay one thousand rupees each month for twenty months. Every month, the whole pool collected from the members goes to one member, so that by the end, every member has received the pool once.

Who gets the money first? In most chit funds, members who need cash urgently bid for it. The pool goes to the member who is willing to give up the largest amount, called the discount. That discount, after the organiser's fee is deducted, is shared among the other members as a kind of dividend, which reduces what each of them pays that month. A member who takes the pool early therefore receives less than he will eventually pay in, while a member who waits until the end receives the full pool after paying less than his full share in most months.

In effect, the chit fund is both a savings scheme and a loan. Early takers borrow from the group and pay for it through the discount; late takers save and are rewarded for their patience. Because members often know one another, the group can judge who is likely to keep paying, something a distant bank cannot easily do.

The arrangement has obvious risks. A member who takes the pool early may stop paying once he has the money. A dishonest organiser may disappear with the collections. For this reason, chit funds in India are regulated by law, and registered funds must follow rules on how they are run. Unregistered schemes, however, continue to operate in many places, and from time to time some of them collapse, leaving members with heavy losses.

Supporters argue that, when it is run honestly, the chit fund offers something that formal finance often does not: credit that is quick, flexible and decided by people who know the borrower. Critics reply that the same informality that makes it useful also makes it dangerous.

stimuli.title: When a fine becomes a fee
stimuli.content:
A group of day-care centres had a familiar problem: some parents arrived late to collect their children, so that teachers had to stay on after closing time. The solution seemed obvious. Introduce a small fine for every late pick-up, and parents would surely become more punctual.

When economists studied what happened after such a fine was introduced at a number of day-care centres in Israel, they found the opposite. The number of late arrivals rose and settled at a higher level than before. More surprising still, when the fine was later withdrawn, lateness did not fall back to its old level.

The researchers offered an explanation that has since become well known. Before the fine, a parent who came late felt that he was imposing on a teacher's goodwill, and that sense of guilt kept most parents on time. The fine changed how the situation was understood. Lateness was no longer a favour taken from a teacher but a service that could be bought, and a modest price for an extra half-hour seemed reasonable to many parents. Once the moral question had been turned into a commercial one, removing the price did not turn it back.

The lesson is not that penalties never work. A fine large enough to hurt will usually change behaviour, and many rules depend on penalties to be obeyed at all. The point is narrower: when people already behave well out of duty, pride or a sense of fairness, a small payment can weaken those motives instead of adding to them. Psychologists sometimes describe this as money 'crowding out' other reasons for acting.

The same risk may appear elsewhere. A small reward for volunteering, for instance, could make the work feel like a poorly paid job rather than a good deed. Policy makers who reach for fines and rewards, therefore, need to ask not only how large an incentive should be, but also what message it sends about the behaviour it is meant to change.

stimuli.title: Profitable but out of cash
stimuli.content:
Ask a shopkeeper whether his business is doing well, and he will probably answer in terms of profit: how much more he sells his goods for than he paid for them. Yet a surprising number of firms that earn a profit on paper close down because they run out of cash. To understand how, it helps to separate two ideas that are easily confused.

Profit measures whether a sale earns more than it costs. Cash measures whether there is money in the bank today to pay the bills that are due today. The two can drift far apart because they move at different times. A wholesaler may pay his supplier on delivery, store the goods for a month, and then sell them to retailers who are allowed sixty days to pay. For three months, the money he has spent is tied up in stock and in amounts owed to him. The sale may be profitable, but in the meantime he must still pay rent, wages and electricity.

Growth makes the problem worse rather than better. Consider a trader who buys goods for ₹80,000 and sells them for ₹1,00,000 on two months' credit. Each such order earns ₹20,000 of profit, but it also locks up ₹80,000 until the buyer pays. If the trader doubles the number of such orders, his expected profit doubles, but so does the cash he must find in advance. A firm that grows faster than its cash can support may collapse at the very moment its order book looks healthiest.

This is why lenders look closely at the working-capital cycle, the time between paying for inputs and receiving cash from customers. Shortening it, by collecting dues faster, holding less stock or negotiating longer credit from suppliers, frees cash without any change in profit. Banks offer overdrafts and short-term loans to bridge the gap, but these carry interest and are best arranged before a crisis arrives, not after.

An old business saying puts the point bluntly: turnover is vanity, profit is sanity, but cash is king. A business can survive for a while without profit; it cannot survive for long without cash.

stimuli.title: Walls that give
stimuli.content:
On a busy road in some Indian cities, you may come across an unusual wall. Rows of hooks and hangers are fixed to it, and on them hang shirts, sweaters, blankets and children's clothes. A painted sign above them carries a simple (1) ______: 'Leave what you do not need; take what you need.'

These 'walls of kindness' are usually started by a few residents or a local group. The rules are few. Anyone who has clean clothes that they no longer wear can hang them up, and anyone who needs them can take them, without asking (2) ______ and without having to explain why. There is no counter, no form to fill in and no one keeping (3) ______ of who gives and who takes.

Supporters say this is exactly what makes the idea work. Many people who badly need a warm blanket in winter feel (4) ______ to stand in a queue and ask for charity. At the wall, they can choose quietly, like any other passer-by. Donors, for their part, find it easier to give when they can simply stop on their way to work.

The walls are not free of problems. Some fill up with torn or dirty clothes that nobody can use, and in the rainy season, clothes left in the open can be (5) ______ within days. Volunteers who look after the walls often sort the clothes every evening and take the unusable ones away.

Still, the idea has spread, and some groups have added shelves for books, toys and shoes. A wall, after all, is usually built to keep people apart. These walls do the (6) ______: they bring together people who might otherwise never meet.

stimuli.title: The mark that will not wash off
stimuli.content:
At every election in India, a voter who has cast her vote leaves the polling station with a small dark line on her left forefinger. It is drawn by a polling official with a special ink, and fingers are checked before anyone is allowed to vote. The mark is a simple but effective (1) ______ against fraud: anyone who tries to vote a second time can be spotted at once, because a finger that already carries the mark gives the game away.

The ink owes its staying power to silver nitrate. When it is applied to the skin and (2) ______ to light, the chemical reacts with the outer layer of the skin and leaves a stain that cannot be removed with soap, oil or ordinary cleaning liquids. The mark does not wash away; it (3) ______ only slowly, as old skin cells are naturally shed and replaced by new ones, a process that usually takes some weeks.

For decades, the ink used in Indian elections has been made by a public-sector company in Karnataka, which also supplies it to a number of other countries for their elections. The exact formula is closely (4) ______, and each batch is tested for quality before it is (5) ______ to polling stations across the country.

Critics sometimes point out that, in an age of electronic voter lists and photo identity cards, such an old-fashioned method seems (6) ______. Election officials reply that its strength lies precisely in its simplicity. It needs no electricity, no network connection and no special training. A glance at a voter's finger is enough to tell whether she has already voted.

stimuli.title: The money left on the card
stimuli.content:
A gift card seems like the perfect present. The buyer does not have to guess the receiver's taste, and the receiver can choose whatever she likes. For the shops that sell them, however, gift cards have an added (1) ______ that is rarely advertised: part of the money loaded on them is never spent.

Some cards are lost in drawers, some are forgotten, and many are used for a purchase that leaves a balance too (2) ______ to bother with. In the retail trade, this unspent money is known as 'breakage'. Because the shop has already received the full amount when the card was sold, every rupee that is never used is, in effect, pure (3) ______.

Shops also gain in less obvious ways. A customer with a card worth one thousand rupees often spends more than that amount, paying the difference from her own pocket. And the money from cards sold before a festival stays with the seller for weeks or months before any goods are handed over, which amounts to an interest-free loan from the buyer.

Consumer groups argue that expiry dates make the problem worse, since a card that (4) ______ after a year turns forgetfulness into a direct gain for the seller. In several countries, rules now limit how soon a gift card may expire or say how unused balances must be treated. The rules differ widely, however, and they are often (5) ______ by buyers who never read the fine print.

None of this means that gift cards are a bad idea. It does mean that the most useful thing a giver can do, after handing over the card, is to remind the receiver to use it before the money quietly disappears.

stimuli.title: Paying for power in advance
stimuli.content:
For decades, electricity in most Indian homes has been paid for after it is used. A meter reader visits, a bill arrives weeks later, and the household pays, or **(1) delays**, as its finances allow. Prepaid smart meters reverse this order. Like a mobile phone, the meter must be recharged before power can be used, and the balance falls as electricity is consumed.

Distribution companies see clear advantages. A large share of their losses comes from bills that are paid late or never paid at all, and from errors in reading meters by hand. A prepaid meter **(2) widens** both gaps: the money arrives in advance, and readings are sent automatically. Supporters add that customers benefit too, since they can track their daily use on a phone and are no longer **(3) surprised** by a large bill at the end of a hot summer month.

The concerns are mostly about poorer households. A family that runs out of balance late at night may find its power cut before it can recharge, which is a serious matter during a heatwave or when a child is unwell. For this reason, many prepaid systems offer a small emergency credit, send repeated alerts as the balance runs low and avoid **(4) restoring** supply at night or on holidays.

There is also a question of trust. When a new meter shows higher readings than the old one, customers often suspect that it is faulty, even when the old meter was simply **(5) overstating** their use. Utilities that install meters without explaining how they work have faced protests in several places.

The technology itself is neither good nor bad. Whether prepaid meters help or hurt depends on how carefully they are **(6) introduced**: with clear information, a fair grace period and a quick way to settle complaints, or with none of these.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what causes presbyopia?

options.text: An infection that spreads in crowded villages
Reading on mobile phones for many hours a day
The lens inside the eye becoming less flexible with age
A poor diet in the years before middle age

solution.concept: Locating a stated cause
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: presbyopia 'happens to almost everyone with age, because the lens inside the eye slowly becomes less flexible.'
steps: The lens becomes less flexible with age
solution.why_others_wrong: Holding a phone further away is a sign of presbyopia, not its cause. The passage says it 'is not a disease', so an infection is wrong. Diet is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The lens inside the eye becoming less flexible with age

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following workers is NOT mentioned in the passage as being affected by weak near vision?

options.text: A weaver following a fine pattern

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 names a tailor, a weaver and a farmer who sorts seeds. A driver is never mentioned; reading distant road signs is not even a near-vision task.
solution.why_others_wrong: The tailor, the weaver and the farmer are all named in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A driver reading road signs

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, which of the following is one reason why some people do not get reading glasses?

options.text: Reading glasses are among the costliest medical aids available.
They believe weak near vision must simply be accepted in old age.
Only doctors in large cities are allowed to test eyesight.
Glasses cannot be worn by people who work outdoors.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'some believe that weak near vision is simply a part of growing old that must be accepted.' Others fear lazy eyes or feel embarrassed.
steps: Find 'The difficulty lies in reaching people'
Belief that it must be accepted
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 3 calls glasses 'among the cheapest of all medical aids', the opposite of costliest. It says a trained health worker can test eyes, so doctors are not required. Outdoor work is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: They believe weak near vision must simply be accepted in old age.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'remedy' as used in the passage ('For an office worker in a city, the remedy is simple')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: remedy = a way of putting a problem right
solution.explanation: The sentence goes on to name what fixes the problem: a visit to an optician and reading glasses. A remedy is a cure or solution.
steps: Context: a visit to an optician and a pair of glasses
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Danger' and 'habit' do not describe a fix. 'Price' is about cost; the sentence names what to do, not what it costs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by the closing words 'years of good work are given back'?

options.text: Old people are given back the jobs they had lost.
Glasses make people feel younger than they really are.
Workers can go on using their skills well for many more years.
People get back the money they spent on eye camps.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a summing-up phrase
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says weak near vision makes skilled workers slow down 'in the very years when their skills are at their best'. Cheap glasses let them see well again, so they can keep working well for years.
steps: Problem: skilled people lose working years
solution.why_others_wrong: No refund of money is mentioned. Nobody is said to have lost a job and got it back. Feeling younger is not suggested; the phrase is about work.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Workers can go on using their skills well for many more years.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage explains a normal change in near vision, shows how it harms the work of village craftspeople and farmers, and describes how cheap glasses restore their working lives.
steps: Para 1: near vision weakens with age
Paras 2-4: the effect on work and why people go without glasses
Para 5: glasses give working years back
solution.why_others_wrong: Presbyopia is 'not a disease'. The passage says glasses are cheap, not costly. City opticians appear in one sentence only.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Seeing Clearly, Working Longer

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why do desire paths appear?

options.text: Children are told to play away from the paved paths.
People in a hurry take the shortest route they can see.
Grass does not grow well near paved paths.
Park managers mark them out for walkers in a hurry.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Most people, when they are in a hurry, take the shortest route they can see.' Cutting corners wears the grass into a path.
steps: Find 'Such paths appear for a simple reason'
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 1 says 'Nobody planned them', so managers did not mark them. Poor grass and children's play are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: People in a hurry take the shortest route they can see.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'faint' as used in the passage ('a faint line becomes visible')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: faint = weak, only just able to be seen
solution.explanation: The line is faint at first and 'within weeks the faint track becomes a clear one'. The contrast with 'clear' shows that faint means only just visible.
solution.why_others_wrong: A path worn by feet is not 'freshly paved' or 'carefully planned' (nobody planned it). 'Very wide' contradicts the narrow strips described in paragraph 1.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a way in which park managers tried to stop walkers?

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists fences, hedges and signs asking people to keep off the grass. Guards and fines are never mentioned.
steps: Guards and fines: not in the passage
solution.why_others_wrong: Fences, hedges and signs are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Posting guards to fine walkers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What do the planners mentioned in paragraph 4 mean when they treat desire paths 'as information'?

options.text: The paths show where people actually want to walk, which helps in planning routes.
The paths prove that most visitors cannot read the signs in the park.
The paths tell managers how many people visit the park each day.
The paths are recorded so that walkers who damage the grass can be identified.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a phrase from the sentence that follows it
solution.explanation: The next sentence explains: 'A path worn across a lawn shows exactly where people want to go.' Planners use this to decide where the paved paths should run.
steps: 'treat them as information' is explained next
Paths show where people want to go
solution.why_others_wrong: Identifying walkers, people's reading ability and visitor counts are never discussed; the passage uses the paths to learn where people want to go.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The paths show where people actually want to walk, which helps in planning routes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: With which of the following statements would the author most probably agree?

options.text: Walkers who cut across lawns should be made to pay for the damage.
Paved paths should never be built in parks or college campuses.
When many users keep ignoring a design, the design should be reconsidered.
Signs and fences are the best way to protect a well-designed park.

solution.concept: Inference: identifying the author's view from the conclusion
solution.explanation: The last paragraph says that when many people keep ignoring a design, 'the fault may lie with the design rather than with the people'. The author favours redrawing routes to follow people.
steps: Para 4: paths treated as useful information
Para 5: fault may lie with the design
solution.why_others_wrong: The author never suggests fining walkers. Paved paths are not rejected, only placed where people walk. Paragraph 3 says fences and signs 'rarely worked for long'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: When many users keep ignoring a design, the design should be reconsidered.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude to desire paths?

options.text: open to learning from them when planning routes
indifferent to how parks and campuses are planned
sad that old gardens are disappearing from cities
angry at the people who damage public lawns

solution.concept: Tone: the author's attitude, judged from the conclusion
solution.explanation: The author presents desire paths as useful information and ends by suggesting that designs may need to follow people. The attitude is open and appreciative.
steps: Conclusion: redraw routes to follow people
Attitude: open to learning from them
solution.why_others_wrong: The author does not blame walkers, so 'angry' is wrong. A writer who discusses planning in detail is not indifferent. Disappearing gardens are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: open to learning from them when planning routes

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the example in the first paragraph, how much is the full monthly pool, before any discount is deducted?

solution.concept: Reading a worked example: pool = number of members × monthly payment
solution.explanation: Twenty members each pay ₹1,000 a month, so the pool collected every month is 20 × ₹1,000 = ₹20,000, and the whole pool goes to one member.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,000 is one member's monthly payment. ₹4,00,000 is the total paid over all twenty months. ₹19,000 leaves out one member's payment for no reason the passage gives.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how is it decided in most chit funds who receives the pool in a given month?

options.text: The organiser chooses the member he trusts most.
The oldest member always receives it first.
Names are drawn by lottery at a monthly meeting.
Members bid, and the one willing to give up the most gets it.

solution.concept: Locating a stated procedure
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: members who need cash 'bid for it. The pool goes to the member who is willing to give up the largest amount, called the discount.'
solution.why_others_wrong: The organiser's choice, a lottery and age are never given as the method in most chit funds.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Members bid, and the one willing to give up the most gets it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the passage say that a member who takes the pool early is, in effect, paying for a loan?

options.text: He has to pay interest to a bank on the amount.
He must pay the organiser's fee twice over.
He receives less than he will pay in over the months.
He is not allowed to take part in later auctions.

solution.concept: Inference: linking the mechanism to the 'savings and loan' idea
solution.explanation: The early taker gives up a discount, so the pool he gets is smaller than the total he will contribute. That difference is the cost of getting the money early, like interest on a loan.
steps: Receives less than he pays in
The gap is the price of early money
solution.why_others_wrong: No double fee or bank interest is mentioned. The passage never says early takers are barred from later auctions; each member simply receives the pool once.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He receives less than he will pay in over the months.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What advantage of the chit fund over a distant bank does the passage point out?

options.text: Its members do not need to pay anything until they receive the pool.
Members know one another and can judge who is likely to keep paying.
It is never affected by dishonest organisers or defaulting members.
It pays a fixed rate of interest that is guaranteed by law.

solution.concept: Inference: identifying a stated contrast
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Because members often know one another, the group can judge who is likely to keep paying, something a distant bank cannot easily do.'
steps: They can judge who will keep paying
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 4 describes dishonest organisers and defaults, so 'never affected' is false. No guaranteed interest is mentioned. Every member pays each month from the start.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Members know one another and can judge who is likely to keep paying.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'collapse' as used in the passage ('from time to time some of them collapse, leaving members with heavy losses')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: collapse = fail suddenly and completely
solution.explanation: A scheme that leaves its members 'with heavy losses' has failed. 'Collapse' here means fail suddenly.
solution.why_others_wrong: Growing, merging or closing for a holiday would not leave members with heavy losses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Banks have now replaced chit funds in every Indian town.
Members who wait until the end of a chit fund always lose money.
Chit funds should be banned because unregistered schemes often collapse.
Chit funds combine saving and borrowing in a way that is useful but risky.

solution.concept: Main idea: balance the mechanism, the benefits and the risks
solution.explanation: The passage explains how a chit fund works, shows that it is both a savings scheme and a loan, describes its risks and ends with the views of supporters and critics.
steps: Para 3: saving plus borrowing; local knowledge
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage never calls for a ban. It says unregistered schemes 'continue to operate', so banks have not replaced them. Paragraph 2 says late takers are 'rewarded for their patience'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Chit funds combine saving and borrowing in a way that is useful but risky.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what happened when the fine for late pick-up was withdrawn?

options.text: Parents began to arrive earlier than before.
Lateness did not fall back to its old level.
The day-care centres stopped staying open late.
Lateness quickly fell back to its old level.

solution.concept: Locating a stated result
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'when the fine was later withdrawn, lateness did not fall back to its old level.'
steps: Did not return to the old level
solution.why_others_wrong: Falling back quickly is the opposite of what the passage says. Earlier arrivals and changed opening hours are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Lateness did not fall back to its old level.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to 'imposing on' as used in the passage ('he was imposing on a teacher's goodwill')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: impose on someone = take unfair advantage of their kindness
solution.explanation: A late parent made a teacher stay on unpaid, relying on her kindness. That is taking unfair advantage of her goodwill, which is why the parent felt guilty.
steps: Context: teacher stays late out of goodwill
solution.why_others_wrong: A parent does not order a teacher, tax her goodwill or praise it; none of these would cause the guilt the passage describes.
solution.final_answer: Option D: taking unfair advantage of

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the researchers' explanation, why did late arrivals increase after the fine was introduced?

options.text: Teachers began to leave earlier, so more parents were counted as late.
Parents who paid the fine were allowed to collect their children at any time.
The fine was too large for most parents to pay, so they stopped caring.
The fine turned lateness into a service that could be bought, easing parents' guilt.

solution.concept: Inference: following the causal chain in an explanation
solution.explanation: Before the fine, guilt about imposing on teachers kept parents punctual. The fine made lateness 'a service that could be bought', and a modest price seemed reasonable, so the guilt that had kept parents on time disappeared.
steps: Before: guilt kept parents on time
Fine: lateness became something one could buy
Guilt gone, price small → more lateness
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage calls the fine 'modest', not too large. Teachers leaving early and unlimited collection times are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The fine turned lateness into a service that could be bought, easing parents' guilt.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: With which of the following statements would the author most probably agree?

options.text: Volunteers always do better work when they are paid a small amount.
Day-care centres should keep their teachers on duty until every child is collected.
A small payment can weaken good behaviour that rests on a sense of duty.
Penalties of any size never change the way people behave.

solution.concept: Inference: distinguishing the author's narrow claim from an overstatement
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says 'The lesson is not that penalties never work', and that 'when people already behave well out of duty, pride or a sense of fairness, a small payment can weaken those motives'.
steps: Narrow point: small payments can crowd out duty
Matches the statement about weakening good behaviour
solution.why_others_wrong: The author says large fines usually work, so 'never change' is wrong. Paragraph 5 suggests a small reward could harm volunteering, the opposite of 'always do better'. Teachers' duty hours are not the author's argument.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A small payment can weaken good behaviour that rests on a sense of duty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: When a Price Replaces a Duty

solution.concept: Title: the central idea, not the example used to illustrate it
solution.explanation: The day-care study is the example; the central idea is that a small fine or payment can replace a moral duty with a commercial deal and so backfire.
steps: Explanation: lateness became something one could buy
General lesson: money can crowd out duty
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage is not about why parents are late in general. It says penalties do not always fail. Earning money for day-care centres is not discussed.
solution.final_answer: Option B: When a Price Replaces a Duty

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the trader's example, if he doubles the number of orders, how much cash must he find in advance to pay for the goods?

solution.concept: Applying a worked example: cash locked up = purchase cost per order × number of orders
solution.explanation: Each order locks up the ₹80,000 paid for the goods until the buyer pays. Doubling the orders doubles this: 2 × ₹80,000 = ₹1,60,000. The passage says the cash he must find in advance doubles along with profit.
steps: Cash locked per order = purchase cost = ₹80,000
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹40,000 is the doubled profit, not the cash needed. ₹2,00,000 is the doubled sale value, which he receives later. ₹80,000 is the need for a single order, before doubling.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, can a fast-growing firm collapse just when its order book looks healthiest?

options.text: Each extra order locks up more cash before customers pay.
Suppliers raise their prices when a firm buys more.
Larger orders always earn a smaller profit per sale.
Banks refuse to lend to firms whose sales are growing.

solution.concept: Inference: the mechanism behind a paradox
solution.explanation: Every order requires paying for goods in advance while the buyer pays later. More orders mean more cash tied up, so a firm can run out of cash even though each order is profitable.
steps: More orders → more cash tied up
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says profit doubles with orders, so profit per sale does not shrink. Banks are said to offer overdrafts, not refuse them. Supplier price rises are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Each extra order locks up more cash before customers pay.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following would free cash for the trader without changing his profit, according to the passage?

options.text: Raising his selling price by ten per cent
Selling more goods on the same credit terms
Paying his suppliers earlier to win their goodwill
Persuading his suppliers to allow him longer credit

solution.concept: Inference: applying the listed remedies to a new case
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists ways to shorten the working-capital cycle 'without any change in profit', including 'negotiating longer credit from suppliers'. Paying later keeps cash with the trader longer.
steps: Remedies: collect faster, hold less stock, longer supplier credit
solution.why_others_wrong: Raising prices changes profit. Selling more on the same terms locks up more cash. Paying suppliers earlier lengthens the cycle and uses up cash.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Persuading his suppliers to allow him longer credit

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Banks That Refuse to Lend to Traders
Why Profitable Firms Can Still Run Out of Money
How to Raise Prices Without Losing Customers

solution.concept: Title: the question the whole passage answers
solution.explanation: The passage opens with firms that are profitable on paper but close for lack of cash, explains why profit and cash differ, shows how growth worsens the gap and ends with 'cash is king'.
steps: Body: profit vs cash, growth, working capital
solution.why_others_wrong: Pricing is not discussed. 'Vanity' appears only in the saying, about turnover, not about large businesses. Banks are described as offering loans, not refusing them.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Why Profitable Firms Can Still Run Out of Money

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what a sign 'carries' when it states an idea
solution.explanation: The sign states the idea of the wall: leave what you do not need, take what you need. A sign that carries such words carries a message.
steps: Words on the sign: an invitation to give and take
solution.why_others_wrong: The wall is free, so a 'price' does not fit. The words are not a 'complaint'. They invite people rather than warn them of danger, so 'warning' does not fit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: taking freely, without anyone's approval
solution.explanation: Anyone who needs the clothes can simply take them, without asking anyone for permission and without explaining why.
solution.why_others_wrong: Asking 'directions', 'the weather' or 'a loan' has nothing to do with taking clothes from a wall.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the fixed phrase 'keep records of'
solution.explanation: Along with 'no counter' and 'no form to fill in', the sentence says nobody notes down who gives and who takes: no one is keeping records of it.
steps: List: no counter, no form, no one keeping ___
'___ of who gives and who takes'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Keeping quiet of', 'keeping promises of' and 'keeping secrets of' who gives and who takes are not idiomatic and do not continue the list of missing paperwork.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the feeling the wall helps people avoid
solution.explanation: At the wall, needy people can 'choose quietly, like any other passer-by'. This helps because many feel ashamed to queue up and ask for charity.
steps: Contrast: queueing for charity vs choosing quietly
Queueing for charity is embarrassing for many
solution.why_others_wrong: If people felt 'eager', 'proud' or 'lucky' to queue for charity, the quiet wall would not be what makes the idea work.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: a problem caused by rain
solution.explanation: The paragraph lists problems. Clothes left in the open during the rainy season get wet and dirty and become useless: they are ruined.
steps: Clothes left out in the rain
solution.why_others_wrong: Ironing and folding are improvements, not problems. Nothing on the wall is sold.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: a contrast with what walls usually do
solution.explanation: A wall is 'usually built to keep people apart'. These walls bring people together, which is the opposite.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Do the same' would mean these walls also keep people apart. 'Do the impossible' and 'do the repairs' do not set up the contrast that follows the colon.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'a ___ against fraud' needs a word meaning protection
solution.explanation: The mark lets officials spot anyone who tries to vote twice, so it protects the election against fraud: it is a safeguard.
steps: It catches people who try to vote twice
solution.why_others_wrong: An 'invitation', a 'reward' or an 'excuse' against fraud makes no sense; the mark prevents fraud.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: confusable '-posed' words; exposed to light = left open to light
solution.explanation: The ink reacts once it is on the skin and left in light. The phrase is 'exposed to light'.
steps: 'applied to the skin and ___ to light'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Opposed to' means against; 'composed' means made up of or calm; 'disposed to' means inclined to. None describes ink being left in light.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'does not wash away; it ___ only slowly' describes gradual disappearance
solution.explanation: The mark disappears gradually as old skin cells are shed. Something that disappears gradually fades.
steps: Gradual loss as skin is replaced
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Spreads', 'darkens' and 'multiplies' describe the mark growing or strengthening, which does not fit skin being shed and replaced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'closely guarded' (kept secret) is a fixed collocation for a formula or secret
solution.explanation: A formula made by only one supplier for decades is kept secret: it is 'closely guarded'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Closely published' is self-contradictory. 'Closely ignored' and 'closely borrowed' are not idiomatic and do not fit a valued formula.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: sending goods 'to polling stations'
solution.explanation: After testing, each batch is sent out to polling stations: it is dispatched to them.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Withheld' means kept back, the opposite of supplying. 'Subjected to' means made to undergo, and ink is not 'borrowed' to polling stations; neither describes sending supplies.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what critics would say about an 'old-fashioned method' in a digital age
solution.explanation: Critics contrast the ink with electronic lists and photo cards, suggesting it belongs to the past: it seems outdated. The officials' reply defends its simplicity.
steps: Contrast: electronic lists vs an old-fashioned ink
Critics' charge: it belongs to the past
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Futuristic' contradicts 'old-fashioned'. 'Compulsory' is not a criticism linked to modern technology. The mark is plainly visible, so 'invisible' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'For the shops ..., however' sets up a benefit to sellers
solution.explanation: Money that is paid for but never spent is a gain for the shop. Gift cards therefore have an added advantage for sellers, one that is 'rarely advertised'.
steps: Unspent money stays with the shop
That is a gain for the seller
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Drawback', 'weakness' and 'nuisance' describe disadvantages, but the colon introduces a gain for shops.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'too ___ to bother with'
solution.explanation: People do not bother with a leftover balance because it is too small to be worth the trouble.
steps: Pattern: too + adjective + to bother with
A balance not worth the effort
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'large', 'valuable' or 'generous' balance is exactly what people would bother to spend.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: money received for which nothing is ever given
solution.explanation: The shop has been paid in full, and if the card is never used it hands over no goods. That money is pure profit.
steps: No goods handed over for unused money
solution.why_others_wrong: For the shop this money is a gain, not a 'loss'. It is not a 'debt' or a 'tax', which the shop would owe to someone.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'expiry dates' in the same sentence decide the verb
solution.explanation: The sentence is about expiry dates: a card that expires after a year cannot be used after that, so a forgotten balance becomes the seller's gain.
steps: A card that stops being valid after a year
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Matures' is used for deposits or bonds that become payable, which would help the holder. 'Multiplies' and 'reopens' do not turn forgetfulness into a gain for the seller.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: confusable 'over-' verbs; overlook = fail to notice
solution.explanation: Buyers 'who never read the fine print' fail to notice the rules: the rules are overlooked by them.
steps: Clue: buyers never read the fine print
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Overseen' means supervised, which buyers do not do. 'Overstated' means exaggerated and 'overtaken' means passed; neither fits people who do not read the rules.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'a bill arrives weeks later, and the household pays, or delays, as its finances allow'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: under post-paid billing, a household short of money pays late
solution.explanation: With a bill paid after use, a household pays when it can, or puts off paying 'as its finances allow'. 'Delays' fits, and it also explains the late payments mentioned in paragraph 2.
steps: 'as its finances allow' → pay now or later
solution.why_others_wrong: A household does not 'double', 'receive' or 'earn' a bill as its finances allow; these do not describe a choice about paying.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'A prepaid meter widens both gaps: the money arrives in advance, and readings are sent automatically'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the explanation after the colon shows both problems are solved
solution.explanation: Money arriving in advance ends late payment, and automatic readings end reading errors. The meter closes both gaps; 'widens' says the opposite.
steps: Gap 1: late or unpaid bills → money now comes in advance
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hides' and 'creates' do not match the solutions listed after the colon. 'Widens' contradicts them, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'they can track their daily use on a phone and are no longer surprised by a large bill at the end of a hot summer month'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: tracking daily use removes the shock of a large bill
solution.explanation: Customers who see their use every day know what they are spending, so a big bill no longer comes as a shock: they are 'no longer surprised'. The word is correct.
steps: Daily tracking → customers know their use
A large bill is no longer unexpected
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No longer pleased by a large bill' and 'no longer informed by a large bill' do not describe a benefit of tracking. 'No longer protected by a large bill' is meaningless.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'many prepaid systems offer a small emergency credit, send repeated alerts as the balance runs low and avoid restoring supply at night or on holidays'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the safeguards protect families from losing power at a bad time
solution.explanation: The concern is power being cut late at night. To protect families, systems avoid cutting off supply at night or on holidays. Avoiding 'restoring' supply would make things worse.
steps: Concern: power cut at night before recharge
Safeguards: credit, alerts, no night cuts
solution.why_others_wrong: Avoiding 'measuring' or 'billing' supply at night does not address the danger described. 'Restoring' reverses the safeguard, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'When a new meter shows higher readings than the old one, customers often suspect that it is faulty, even when the old meter was simply overstating their use'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: higher new readings are explained by an old meter that recorded too little
solution.explanation: If the new meter reads higher and is accurate, the old one must have been recording less than the real use: it was understating it. An old meter that overstated use would have shown higher readings, not lower.
steps: New meter accurate → old meter read too low
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Displaying' and 'doubling' do not explain why the old readings were lower. 'Overstating' gives the reverse logic, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (6) may be wrongly used: 'Whether prepaid meters help or hurt depends on how carefully they are introduced'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the colon lists features of a careful roll-out
solution.explanation: Clear information, a grace period and quick complaint handling describe how the meters are brought in. 'Introduced' is correct.
steps: After the colon: information, grace period, complaints
solution.why_others_wrong: Meters that are 'abandoned', 'disconnected' or 'forgotten' are not being rolled out with information and a grace period.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
May I lend your pen (A) / for a minute? (B) / Mine has run out of ink. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Mine has run out of ink.

solution.concept: Lend = give for a time; borrow = take for a time
solution.explanation: The speaker wants to take and use someone else's pen for a minute, so the verb is 'borrow': 'May I borrow your pen for a minute?' One lends something to another person.
steps: The speaker will take the pen
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct time phrase. Part C correctly gives the reason. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: May I lend your pen

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
An one-day workshop (A) / was organised (B) / for new account holders. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'A' or 'an' depends on the first sound: 'one' begins with a 'w' sound, so it takes 'a'
solution.explanation: 'One' is pronounced with a consonant sound /w/, so the article is 'a': 'A one-day workshop was organised ...'.
steps: 'An one-day' → 'A one-day': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct singular passive verb. Part C is a correct purpose phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Before filing his return, (A) / he took (B) / some useful advise from a tax consultant. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: some useful advise from a tax consultant.

solution.concept: Advice (noun, the 'c' form) vs advise (verb, the 's' form)
solution.explanation: After 'some useful', a noun is needed. The noun is 'advice'; 'advise' is the verb ('to advise someone'). Correct: 'he took some useful advice from a tax consultant.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct participle phrase. Part B is a correct past tense. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: some useful advise from a tax consultant.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
At the staff meeting, (A) / the news of the merger (B) / were announced by the chairman. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'News' looks plural but is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'News' is singular in meaning and grammar: 'the news of the merger was announced by the chairman.'
steps: 'were announced' → 'was announced': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct place phrase. Part B is a correct subject; 'of the merger' does not change its number. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: were announced by the chairman.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Two masked men (A) / robbed fifty thousand rupees (B) / from the cash van. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Rob a person or place (of something); steal a thing (from someone)
solution.explanation: The object here is the money, the thing taken, so the verb is 'steal': 'Two masked men stole fifty thousand rupees from the cash van.' One robs a van or a bank, not the money.
steps: Object: fifty thousand rupees (the thing taken)
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject. Part C correctly uses 'from' with the place the money was taken from. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: robbed fifty thousand rupees

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The customer to whom (A) / the cheque was issued (B) / has not yet deposited it. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Whom' as the object of a preposition ('to whom'); present perfect with 'not yet'
solution.explanation: 'To whom' is correct because 'whom' is the object of 'to' (the cheque was issued to him). 'Has not yet deposited it' agrees with the singular 'The customer' and uses the present perfect with 'yet'.
steps: Part C: singular subject, 'has not yet deposited': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Afraid of losing his job, (A) / the junior clerk dare not to complain (B) / about his long hours. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the junior clerk dare not to complain

solution.concept: 'Dare not' used as a modal takes a bare infinitive (dare not complain), like 'must not' or 'need not'
solution.explanation: In the negative modal form, 'dare' has no '-s' and is followed directly by the base verb: 'the junior clerk dare not complain'. (As a main verb the pattern is 'does not dare (to) complain'.) 'Dare not to complain' mixes the two.
steps: 'dare not to complain' → 'dare not complain': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct adjective phrase with 'of' + -ing. Part C is a correct prepositional phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: the junior clerk dare not to complain

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Once the auditors (A) / finish to check the vouchers, (B) / the branch can close its books. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the branch can close its books.

solution.concept: 'Finish' takes a gerund (-ing form) as its object, never a to-infinitive
solution.explanation: 'Finish' is followed by the -ing form: 'Once the auditors finish checking the vouchers, the branch can close its books.'
steps: 'finish to check' → 'finish checking': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct start to a time clause; the present tense 'finish' is right for a future time after 'once'. Part C is a correct main clause. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: finish to check the vouchers,

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
After a two-month inquiry, (A) / the clerk who forged the signatures (B) / has been charged of cheating. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the clerk who forged the signatures

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: charged WITH an offence (but accused OF an offence)
solution.explanation: The verb 'charge' in the legal sense takes 'with': 'the clerk ... has been charged with cheating.' 'Of' belongs with 'accused'.
steps: 'charged of' → 'charged with': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time phrase. Part B is a correct subject with a relative clause. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: has been charged of cheating.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The premises of the old branch (A) / are being converted (B) / into a training centre. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The premises of the old branch

solution.concept: 'Premises' (a building and its land) is always plural in form and takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'Premises' in this sense has no singular form and takes a plural verb, so 'The premises ... are being converted' is correct. 'Converted into' is the right preposition.
steps: Part A: 'premises' = the building and its grounds
Part B: plural verb 'are being converted': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. 'Is being converted' would be wrong, because 'premises' takes a plural verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Despite the bank cut its rates twice, (A) / demand for home loans (B) / remained weak through the year. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Despite the bank cut its rates twice,

solution.concept: 'Despite' is a preposition: it takes a noun or -ing form, not a full clause
solution.explanation: A full clause ('the bank cut its rates') cannot follow 'despite'. Correct forms: 'Despite the bank's cutting its rates twice', 'Despite two rate cuts by the bank', or 'Although the bank cut its rates twice, ...'.
steps: A preposition cannot take a clause with a finite verb
'Despite the bank cut' → 'Although the bank cut': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct subject. Part C is a correct verb with an adjective complement. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Despite the bank cut its rates twice,

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The borrower did not repay the loan, (A) / nor he replied (B) / to any of the bank's notices. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The borrower did not repay the loan,
to any of the bank's notices.

solution.concept: After 'nor' introducing a clause, the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion)
solution.explanation: 'Nor' at the start of a clause works like a negative adverb, so the subject and auxiliary are inverted: '..., nor did he reply to any of the bank's notices.'
steps: Inversion: nor + auxiliary + subject + base verb
'nor he replied' → 'nor did he reply': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct negative clause. Part C correctly uses 'reply to'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Little did the clerk realise (A) / that the customer he had helped (B) / was the bank's new chairman. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: that the customer he had helped

solution.concept: Inversion after the negative adverb 'Little' (= not at all); past perfect for the earlier action
solution.explanation: 'Little did the clerk realise' correctly inverts the auxiliary 'did' and the subject after 'Little' used in a negative sense. 'He had helped' is correctly earlier than 'realise', and 'was' agrees with 'the customer'.
steps: Part A: Little + did + subject + base verb: correct
Part B: past perfect for the earlier action: correct
Part C: singular 'was' with 'the customer': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. 'Little the clerk realised' would be the error, not the inverted form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new app is both faster (A) / and it is easier to use (B) / than the old one. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The new app is both faster
and it is easier to use

solution.concept: Correlative 'both ... and' must join items of the same grammatical type (parallelism)
solution.explanation: 'Both' comes before an adjective ('faster'), so 'and' must also be followed by an adjective: 'The new app is both faster and easier to use than the old one.' 'And it is easier' adds a whole clause.
steps: 'and it is easier' → 'and easier': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly places 'both' before the first adjective. Part C completes the comparison correctly. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: and it is easier to use

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The auditors found that the manager had approved (A) / large loans to two firms (B) / which his brother was a director. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The auditors found that the manager had approved
which his brother was a director.

solution.concept: In a relative clause, the preposition needed by the verb or noun cannot be dropped (a director OF which)
solution.explanation: His brother was a director 'of' the firms, so the relative clause needs 'of which': '... large loans to two firms of which his brother was a director.'
steps: Underlying idea: his brother was a director OF the firms
'which his brother' → 'of which his brother': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses the past perfect after 'found'. Part B is a correct object phrase. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: which his brother was a director.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The tea in the canteen was **very hot to drink**, so he waited for it to cool.

solution.concept: 'Too + adjective + to-infinitive' shows that something is more than is acceptable for the action
solution.explanation: The tea was hotter than he could drink, so he waited. Excess that prevents an action is shown by 'too ... to': 'The tea ... was too hot to drink.'
steps: Meaning: hot enough to stop him drinking
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Very hot for drinking' and 'so hot to drink' do not express excess correctly ('so' needs 'that': so hot that he could not drink it). The original uses 'very', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: too hot to drink

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**The both brothers** run the family's grain shop together.

solution.concept: 'Both' comes before the article: both the + plural noun (never 'the both')
solution.explanation: 'Both' is placed before 'the', not after it: 'Both the brothers (or Both brothers) run the family's grain shop together.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'The both of brothers' keeps the wrong order and adds 'of' without a pronoun. 'Both brother' needs a plural noun. The original puts 'the' before 'both', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Ramesh visited the branch **for withdrawing** money from his pension account.

solution.concept: A person's purpose in doing something is expressed by the to-infinitive (infinitive of purpose)
solution.explanation: Ramesh's purpose in visiting the branch is shown with 'to': 'Ramesh visited the branch to withdraw money from his pension account.' ('For + -ing' describes what a thing is used for, as in 'a form for withdrawing money'.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'For to withdraw' and 'for withdraw' are ungrammatical. 'For withdrawing' describes the use of a thing, not a person's purpose, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Customers should **pay attention towards** the fine print before signing a loan agreement.

solution.concept: Fixed collocation: pay attention to (something)
solution.explanation: The noun 'attention' with 'pay' takes 'to': 'Customers should pay attention to the fine print ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'At' and 'on' are not used after 'pay attention', and 'towards' is not standard here either, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The new branch is **twice as larger as** the old one.

solution.concept: Multiplier comparisons use 'as + base adjective + as' (twice as large as)
solution.explanation: In 'as ... as' comparisons the adjective stays in its base form, with the multiplier in front: 'The new branch is twice as large as the old one.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Twice larger as' mixes a comparative with 'as'. 'Two times as larger than' mixes both patterns. The original uses a comparative inside 'as ... as', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: twice as large as

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
After paying the school fees, I **have no any money** left for this month.

solution.concept: 'No' and 'any' are not used together; use 'no + noun' or 'not ... any + noun'
solution.explanation: 'No' already makes the sentence negative, so 'any' cannot follow it: 'I have no money left' (or 'I do not have any money left').
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Any no money' is ungrammatical, and 'not no money' is a double negative. The original combines 'no' and 'any', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
She **would rather walk** to the branch than wait for the bus in the heat.

solution.concept: 'Would rather' + bare infinitive (... than + bare infinitive) for a preference
solution.explanation: 'Would rather' is followed by the base form of the verb, and so is 'than': 'She would rather walk to the branch than wait for the bus in the heat.' The sentence is correct.
steps: Followed by the base verb: walk
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Would rather walking' uses an -ing form, and 'would rather to walk' and 'had rather to walk' add 'to'; all three break the pattern.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Unlike the old branch**, the new branch's vault has two separate locks.

solution.concept: 'Unlike' must compare like with like: the thing after 'unlike' must be the same kind of thing as the subject
solution.explanation: The subject is 'the new branch's vault', so it must be compared with a vault, not with a branch: 'Unlike the old branch's vault, the new branch's vault has two separate locks.'
steps: Subject compared: the new branch's vault
'Unlike the old branch' compares a vault with a branch
Compare vault with vault: 'Unlike the old branch's vault'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unlike in the old branch's' leaves the possessive without a noun, and 'Unlike with the old branch' adds a preposition and still compares a branch with a vault. The original is a faulty comparison, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Unlike the old branch's vault

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
It took the old clerk almost a month to **get on** his fever.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: get over (an illness or a shock) = recover from it
solution.explanation: Recovering from a fever is 'getting over' it: 'It took the old clerk almost a month to get over his fever.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Get off' means leave a vehicle or escape punishment. 'Get by' means manage with little. 'Get on' means board or make progress; none means recover, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The branch manager **dealt in** the customer's complaint within a day.

solution.concept: Deal with = handle or take action on; deal in = trade in (goods)
solution.explanation: A manager who handles a complaint 'deals with' it: 'The branch manager dealt with the customer's complaint within a day.' 'Deal in' is used for trading, as in 'He deals in spices'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Dealt by' and 'dealt at' are not idiomatic. 'Dealt in' means traded in, which does not fit a complaint, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: He and I went to the branch together.
Him and me went to the branch together.
He and me went to the branch together.
Me and him went to the branch together.

solution.concept: Pronouns in a compound subject take the subject form (I, he), not the object form (me, him)
solution.explanation: Both pronouns are the subject of 'went', so both take the subject case: 'He and I went to the branch together.' Test each pronoun alone: 'He went', 'I went'.
solution.why_others_wrong: The others use the object forms 'him' or 'me' as subjects, which fails the test of saying each pronoun alone with 'went'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: He and I went to the branch together.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: Give the form to whoever ask for it.
Give the form to whomever asks for it.
Give the form to anyone whom asks for it.
Give the form to whoever asks for it.

solution.concept: The case of 'who(ever)' depends on its role inside its own clause, not on the preposition before the clause
